questions.question: How do you write a FizzBuzz program in Java?
questions.title: FizzBuzz Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **FizzBuzz**: print 1..n, but print **Fizz** for multiples of 3, **Buzz** for multiples of 5, and **FizzBuzz** for multiples of both (i.e. 15). The trap is **order**: check **15 (both) first**, then 3, then 5. Even cleaner is to **build a string** by appending 'Fizz' if divisible by 3 and 'Buzz' if by 5, printing the number only if the string is empty.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you handle the both-multiples case correctly and avoid redundant divisibility checks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking 3 and 5 before the combined 15 case, so 15 prints 'Fizz' instead of 'FizzBuzz'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the string-append approach to avoid the ordering bug and keep it extensible

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Multiples of **3 -> Fizz**, **5 -> Buzz**, **both (15) -> FizzBuzz**.
- Check the **combined case first** in if-else order.
- The **string-build** approach avoids the ordering trap and is extensible.
- Loop `1..n` inclusive; **O(n)** time.
- It's a screen for clean conditional logic, not algorithmic depth.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: FizzBuzz is a classic warm-up. I print the numbers from one to n, but for multiples of three I print Fizz, for multiples of five I print Buzz, and for multiples of both, which is multiples of fifteen, I print FizzBuzz. The important detail is handling the both-multiples case correctly, because there is a subtle ordering trap. If I write the if-else with the modulo-three check first, then fifteen satisfies it and prints Fizz, and it never reaches the FizzBuzz case. So in the if-else style, I check the combined case first, either modulo fifteen equals zero or divisible by both three and five, then check three, then five, then fall back to printing the number. A clean alternative is to build the output string from independent rules. I start with an empty string, append Fizz if the number is divisible by three, append Buzz if it's divisible by five, and then at the end, if the string is still empty I print the number, otherwise I print the string. This naturally handles fifteen, because both appends fire and I get FizzBuzz, and there's no ordering to get wrong. It's also more extensible: if someone adds a new rule, like print Bazz for multiples of seven, I just add one more append line instead of rewriting a tangle of nested conditionals. It is O of n, and the rule-building version stays easy to extend without a tangle of conditionals.

sections.title: Independent divisibility rules
sections.content:
FizzBuzz prints one result for each number from 1 through `n`: `Fizz` for multiples of 3, `Buzz` for multiples of 5, `FizzBuzz` for multiples of both, and the number otherwise.

The direct conditional version must test divisibility by both numbers before testing either one alone. At 15, both `15 % 3 == 0` and `15 % 5 == 0` are true. If the multiple-of-3 branch comes first in an `if/else if` chain, it prints only `Fizz` and the later combined case is never reached.

**Worked example: 13 through 16**

- 13 matches no rule, so print `13`.
- 14 matches no rule, so print `14`.
- 15 matches both, so print `FizzBuzz`.
- 16 matches no rule, so print `16`.

Another clean version builds a string: append `Fizz` when divisible by 3 and append `Buzz` when divisible by 5. If the string is empty, print the number. This version naturally combines rules and is easier to extend with another divisor.

The program performs constant work for each of `n` numbers, so it takes O(n) time. Apart from output, it uses O(1) extra space. Handle `n <= 0` according to the method contract, usually by producing no output.

sections.title: FizzBuzz (String-Build Approach)
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[i from 1 to n] --> B[out = empty]
    B --> C{i % 3 == 0?}
    C -- yes --> D[out += Fizz]
    C -- no --> E[skip]
    D --> F{i % 5 == 0?}
    E --> F
    F -- yes --> G[out += Buzz]
    F -- no --> H[skip]
    G --> I{out empty?}
    H --> I
    I -- yes --> J[print i]
    I -- no --> K[print out]
```

sections.title: Buggy order - 15 prints 'Fizz'
Correct - check both first, or build a string
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrong order**: checking `% 3` before the combined case makes 15 print `Fizz`.
- **Redundant checks**: `% 3 && % 5` is the same as `% 15` - either is fine, just be consistent.
- **Off-by-one**: loop must be `1..n` inclusive.
- **Hard to extend**: nested if-else gets messy if rules grow (7 -> 'Bazz'); the string approach scales.

questions.question: How do you check if a number is prime in Java?
questions.title: Prime Number Check Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **prime** has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. To test `n`, check divisibility only up to **sqrt(n)** - if no number in `2..sqrt(n)` divides `n`, it's prime. That's **O(sqrt(n))**, far better than checking up to `n`. Handle edge cases: numbers `< 2` are not prime. To find all primes up to n, use the **Sieve of Eratosthenes** in O(n log log n).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you optimize the loop to sqrt(n) and handle n < 2 correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Looping all the way to n (O(n)) or to n/2, and mishandling 0, 1, and 2
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why sqrt(n) suffices (factors pair up) and mention the Sieve for ranges

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Prime = exactly **two divisors** (1 and itself), `> 1`.
- Check divisors only up to **sqrt(n)** -> **O(sqrt(n))**.
- Factors pair as `d` and `n/d`; one is `<= sqrt(n)`.
- Handle **n < 2** as not prime.
- For all primes up to n, use the **Sieve of Eratosthenes**.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A prime number is a natural number greater than one that has exactly two divisors, one and itself. The naive way to test if n is prime is to try dividing it by every number from two up to n minus one, but that's O of n and wasteful. The important optimization is to only check divisors up to the square root of n. The reason that works is that divisors come in pairs: if some number d divides n, then n divided by d also divides n, and for any such pair, at least one of the two is less than or equal to the square root of n. So if I haven't found any divisor by the time I reach the square root, there can't be one above it either, which means n is prime. That brings the time down to O of square root of n. I also handle the edge cases up front: anything less than two, that's zero, one, and negative numbers, is not prime, so I return false immediately. In the loop, instead of computing Math dot sqrt, which can have floating-point rounding issues, I just continue while i times i is less than or equal to n, and I cast to long to avoid overflow for large values. If the question is instead to find all the primes up to some n, I wouldn't test each one individually; I'd use the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which marks multiples of each prime as composite and runs in about O of n log log n, much faster for a whole range.

sections.title: Divisors only need to reach the square root
sections.content:
A prime number is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Numbers below 2 are not prime, and 2 is the smallest prime.

To test `n`, try possible divisors only while `d <= n / d`, which is an overflow-safe form of `d * d <= n`. If `n` has a factor larger than its square root, the matching factor must be smaller than the square root and would already have been found.

**Worked example: `29`**

The square root of 29 is a little above 5, so test 2, 3, 4, and 5. None divides 29 exactly, so 29 is prime. For 35, divisor 5 gives remainder zero, so return false immediately; there is no reason to test later values.

After handling 2, an optimized loop can test only odd divisors `3, 5, 7, ...`. This halves unnecessary checks but does not change the O(√n) complexity. The method uses O(1) extra space.

Do not loop all the way to `n - 1`, which is O(n). Also avoid `i * i <= n` with large `int` values unless multiplication is widened to `long`, because integer overflow can make the condition incorrect.

sections.title: Primality Test Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[n] --> B{n < 2?}
    B -- yes --> X[not prime]
    B -- no --> C[i = 2]
    C --> D{i*i <= n?}
    D -- no --> P[prime]
    D -- yes --> E{n % i == 0?}
    E -- yes --> X
    E -- no --> F[i++]
    F --> D
```

sections.title: Primality in O(sqrt n) with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Looping to n or n/2**: only need up to **sqrt(n)** - factors pair up.
- **Mishandling < 2**: 0, 1, and negatives are **not** prime; return false early.
- **Overflow in `i*i`**: cast to `long` for large `n`.
- **`Math.sqrt` rounding**: prefer `i * i <= n` to avoid floating-point off-by-one.

questions.question: How do you find the second largest element in an array?
questions.title: Second Largest Element Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: For the **second distinct largest** value, keep `largest` and `second` during one scan. A new maximum moves the old maximum into second place; another value updates second only when it lies strictly between them. This is O(n) time and O(1) space. State whether duplicates count, and return an explicit no-answer result when the array has fewer than two distinct values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you do it in one pass with two trackers instead of sorting, handling duplicates
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting (O(n log n)) when O(n) works, or returning a duplicate of the max as the second largest
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State whether second means distinct and return an explicit no-answer result when fewer than two distinct values exist

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Define whether the result must be the **second distinct** value.
- Track `largest` and `second` in one **O(n)** pass.
- A new maximum shifts the old maximum into second place.
- Use a safe presence flag or a `long` sentinel for `int` input.
- Return an explicit empty result when two distinct values do not exist.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I would first clarify whether the question means the second distinct largest value. For that version, I can avoid sorting and scan once with two trackers. When a number is greater than `largest`, the old largest moves to `second` and the new value becomes largest. Otherwise, a value updates second only when it is below largest but above the current second. For example, in `[5, 1, 5, 3, 4]`, the repeated 5 is ignored, 3 replaces 1, and 4 becomes the answer. This gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space instead of O(n log n) sorting. I would not silently return `Integer.MIN_VALUE` for `[7, 7]`, because that value can also be a valid array element. A simple implementation can hold the `int` values in `long` trackers initialized to `Long.MIN_VALUE`, then return `OptionalInt.empty()` when the second tracker was never set. That makes the no-answer case explicit and still handles every possible integer input.

sections.title: Track two distinct maximums in one pass
sections.content:
Keep `largest` and `second` as the two greatest distinct values seen so far. When a value is greater than `largest`, move the old largest into second place and replace it. Otherwise, update `second` only when the value is smaller than `largest` but greater than the current second.

**Worked example: `[5, 1, 5, 3, 4]`**

After 5, `largest` is 5. Value 1 becomes second. The next 5 is equal to the largest, so it is ignored when the requirement is the second distinct largest. Value 3 replaces 1, and value 4 replaces 3. The answer is 4, not 5.

Clarify whether “second largest” means distinct. If duplicates count as separate positions, `[5, 5, 4]` may return 5; most interview versions ask for the second distinct value. An array with fewer than two distinct values, such as `[7, 7]`, has no answer and should return an optional value or throw a documented exception rather than a misleading sentinel.

One scan gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Sorting also works in O(n log n), but it changes the array unless copied and does more work than needed. Using nullable wrappers or explicit flags avoids collision with a real `Integer.MIN_VALUE` input.

sections.title: Two-tracker scan
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[largest and second are unset] --> B{next x?} B -- no --> Z{second set?} Z -- yes --> R[return second] Z -- no --> N[no distinct second value] B -- yes --> C{x greater than largest?} C -- yes --> D[second = largest if set
largest = x] C -- no --> E{x below largest and
greater than second?} E -- yes --> F[second = x] E -- no --> G[ignore duplicate or smaller value] D --> B F --> B G --> B ```

sections.title: Sorting - works but O(n log n)
Single pass with an explicit no-answer result
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sorting unnecessarily:** O(n log n) when one O(n) scan works.
- **Counting a duplicate maximum:** decide whether the result must be distinct.
- **Starting at zero:** that fails for all-negative arrays.
- **Using `Integer.MIN_VALUE` as both data and 'missing':** the value is legal input, so use a separate presence rule.
- **Ignoring no-answer input:** `[7, 7]` has no second distinct value.

questions.question: How do you rotate an array by k positions in Java?
questions.title: Rotate Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Rotate right by k using the **reversal trick** in O(n) time, **O(1)** space: first **`k %= n`** (k can exceed n), then **reverse the whole array**, **reverse the first k**, and **reverse the rest**. The three reversals leave the array rotated right by k. The naive 'shift one position k times' is O(n*k); an extra-array copy is O(n) time but O(n) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the in-place reversal algorithm and the k %= n normalization
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting k %= n (k > n loops), or using O(n) extra space when O(1) is possible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Derive the three-reversal trick and handle k > n with the modulo up front

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Normalize with **`k %= n`** first.
- **Three reversals**: whole, first k, last n-k -> rotate right by k.
- **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.
- Beats the O(n) extra-array copy and O(n*k) shifting.
- For rotate **left** by k, rotate right by `n - k` (or reverse in the other order).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To rotate an array to the right by k, the slick in-place approach uses three reversals. But before anything, I normalize k by taking k modulo n, because rotating by the array's length is a no-op, and k might be larger than the array. Then the algorithm is: reverse the entire array, then reverse just the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n minus k elements. After those three steps, the array is rotated right by k, and it's done in O of n time and O of one space, completely in place. The intuition is that reversing the whole array brings the last k elements to the front, but they end up in reverse order, and reversing each of the two pieces afterward restores their correct internal order. Let me give a quick example. With one through five and k equals two, reversing the whole thing gives five, four, three, two, one. Reversing the first two gives four, five, three, two, one. Then reversing the last three gives four, five, one, two, three, which is exactly the original rotated right by two. The mistakes to avoid are forgetting the k modulo n step, which breaks when k is greater than or equal to n, and getting the segment boundaries wrong, the first segment is index zero to k minus one and the second is k to n minus one. There are other approaches, copying into a new array is O of n space, and shifting one position at a time k times is O of n times k, which is far too slow, so the reversal trick is the one I reach for. To rotate left by k instead, I just rotate right by n minus k.

sections.title: Why three reversals perform a rotation
sections.content:
Think of the array as two parts: `A` contains the first `n - k` elements and `B` contains the last `k`. A right rotation changes `A B` into `B A`.

Reversing the complete array produces `reverse(B) reverse(A)`. Reversing those two parts separately restores the order inside each part, leaving exactly `B A`.

**Worked example**

For `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` and `k = 2`, `A = [1, 2, 3]` and `B = [4, 5]`. Reverse everything to get `[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]`. Reverse indexes 0 through 1 to get `[4, 5, 3, 2, 1]`. Reverse indexes 2 through 4 to get `[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]`, which is the required right rotation.

Normalize `k` with `k %= n` so rotating by 7 positions in a five-element array behaves like rotating by 2. Handle an empty array before that calculation to avoid division by zero. If negative rotations are allowed, normalize with `((k % n) + n) % n`.

Every element participates in a constant number of swaps, so the method is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

sections.title: Three-Reversal Rotation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[k = k % n] --> B[reverse whole array]
    B --> C[reverse first k]
    C --> D[reverse last n-k]
    D --> Z[rotated right by k]
```

sections.title: Rotate by k with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `k %= n`**: when `k > n` (or `k == n`), indices break or you do useless work.
- **Wrong segment bounds**: first segment is `[0, k-1]`, second is `[k, n-1]`.
- **O(n) extra space**: the reversal method is O(1); don't copy unless asked.
- **O(n*k) shifting**: rotating one position at a time is far too slow for large k.
